sentences: A month after his party-obsessed wife the socialite left him, the writer's father the old man tells the writer that he has stopped chemotherapy because "tough guys don't dance".
The writer reveals in turn that there are parts of two murdered bodies in his cellar, and that while he doesn't think that he murdered them, he has been suffering from blackouts and hallucinations.
Five days earlier, the writer spent the night doing cocaine and having sex with pornographic film actress the actress in front of her partner the companion.
He awoke to discover bloody clothing in his car and the name of his former girlfriend the old flame tattooed on his arm.

When the new town police chief the lawman, now married to the old flame, warned the writer to remove his marijuana stash from the woods before state troopers found it, the writer discovered a severed head hidden in the stash.
The lawman tells the writer that the companion committed suicide and the actress is missing.
In a flashback, the writer remembers meeting the old flame when he was a bartender, then meeting the socialite and encouraging the old flame to swing with her and husband the first husband.
The socialite promised to get rid of the first husband, marry and then divorce a rich man for his money, then marry the writer to finance his dreams of being a writer.
An argument between the writer and the old flame while driving caused their car to crash, rendering the old flame infertile.
Later, after spending time in prison for dealing cocaine, the writer reunited with the socialite who'd married her rich man, the writer's former classmate the millionaire.
She convinced him to hire the writer as the socialite's chauffeur then filed for divorce.
The writer testified against the millionaire to help her get a large settlement.
The day before the film's opening, the writer reunited with the old flame.
She tells him the lawman and the socialite are having an affair and suggests killing them.
That night, the lawman tells the writer he thought the companion and the actress had been sent to buy cocaine from him with $2 million provided by the socialite and the millionaire.
The lawman suspects the writer murdered the companion and the actress.
The writer goes to check his stash and discovers there are now two severed heads, and is assaulted by his friends the first friend and the second friend before escaping with the heads.
The old man disposes of the heads, which are the socialite's and the actress's, at sea.
The writer is kidnapped by the millionaire, who admits to sending the first friend and the second friend to assault him before killing them both.
The writer is taken to the abandoned settlement where the first friend, the second friend, the socialite and the actress are buried.

The millionaire tells the writer that he and the socialite had sent the actress and the companion to buy cocaine from the lawman, but the actress shot the companion when he threatened to leave with the money.
When the socialite and the lawman arrived, the actress threatened to turn them both in, but was shot by the socialite.
The lawman took the money, hid the actress's head, and had sex with the socialite.
The millionaire shot the socialite after she revealed that there never was any cocaine, that she and the lawman had scammed him, and that they were blackmailing him for an additional $10 million.
After these confessions, the millionaire shoots himself.
The writer finds the old flame waiting outside his home, and they kiss.
The lawman drunkenly admits to framing the writer as revenge for what he did to the old flame, and to being in love with the socialite.
The writer tells the lawman the socialite is dead and he suffers a stroke.
While recovering in bed, the lawman taunts the old flame as inferior to the socialite, and the old flame shoots him.
The writer and the old man dispose of the seven bodies at sea, and the old flame uses the $2 million to buy a house for her and the writer.

The matriarch, stepmother to the three family children – the eldest stepson, the younger stepson, and the stepdaughter – and mother to the daughter, blackmails the family lawyer, the attorney, into destroying her late husband's second will that would split his fortune between her and his children, leaving them $200,000 each, freeing them from her controlling presence.
The original will leaves all of the family fortune to the matriarch, only splitting it evenly amongst the children upon her death.
She takes the stepchildren and the daughter-in-law, the eldest stepson's wife who serves as the matriarch's nurse, on holiday to the continent.
In the port city, the great detective the sleuth runs into an old friend, the doctor.
The doctor soon falls in love with the younger stepson, to the matriarch's disapproval.
The noblewoman is introduced.
She was born American but has had British nationality for the last ten years due to marriage, during which she became a member of parliament.
She, archaeologist the scholar, and lawyer the attorney are also on their way to the holy city and the dig site.
The family are surprised to see the attorney on the ship.
The adult step-children discover the existence of a second will their father told the eldest stepson about before he died.
The matriarch continues to bully her step-children.
The attorney is flirting with the daughter-in-law who overtly accepts his courting.
He also resists the matriarch's demand that he stay away from them.

The matriarch poisons the attorney's wine with her digitalis medication, but the wine is spilled when the daughter-in-law's husband strikes the attorney, having found an engraved cigarette case which the attorney had given her.
The sleuth observes several cockroaches drinking from the spill and dying, and keeps a close eye on the family when they disembark.

At the archaeological dig, the attorney, the daughter-in-law, the eldest stepson, the stepdaughter, the younger stepson and the doctor go for a walk, but the eldest stepson turns back, upset by his wife's preference for the attorney.
Later the others return one by one.
The doctor notices an Arab man trying to wake the matriarch.
When she goes over, she finds the matriarch dead.
The doctor examines the body and identifies the cause of death as heart failure, but the sleuth points out it is wise to be suspicious when there is a death of someone who is widely hated.
He asks the doctor to check her medical bag and she finds it disordered, with an empty bottle of digitalis and a syringe missing.

The sleuth deduces that the matriarch was injected with a lethal dose of digitalis, corresponding to a medicine she took administered by two drops in a glass of water by the daughter-in-law, in order that her death appear to be by heart failure.
Since the family could have injected the digitalis without needing an additional syringe, he suspects an outsider.
The sleuth arranges to meet with a local youth who witnessed the murder, but he never arrives, scared off by an unknown third party.
The doctor chases him through the streets, passing by many of the family members and the noblewoman.
As she catches the boy, a gun is fired and the boy is killed.
The doctor is arrested, but claims he was shot before her eyes by an unseen assailant.
The sleuth has her released so she can travel with him to meet the others for a 'picnic' where he plans to reveal what happened.

Having suggested that all the step-children lied about seeing their step-mother alive when she was actually dead (thinking one of them may have done it and wishing to delay or protect them against discovery), the sleuth clears them of suspicion.
At a banquet later that night, the sleuth reveals the truth: the noblewoman is the murderer.
She was once in prison and the matriarch had recognised her from her time as a prison warden.
To keep her quiet and maintain her status, the noblewoman injected the matriarch with digitalis from the doctor's bag and silenced the witness.
Disturbed by the revelation, the noblewoman flees to her room.
During a fireworks show following the banquet, the noblewoman shoots herself in her hotel room, not willing to return to prison.
The sleuth persuades the local authorities to consider her death an accident, not wanting to disparage the late Lady's reputation further.
On New Year's Eve, borough socialite the wealthy woman returns home from the evening's festivities.
As she feeds her fish before going to bed, a killer uses a blue ribbon to strangle her to death.
It is the latest murder by a serial killer who has been terrorizing the city for eleven months.
The mayor, frustrated with the lack of progress in the case, tells city police commissioner the commissioner to bring in his brother, former detective the detective.
This is a controversial decision, as the detective left the force in disgrace two years earlier but may be the only police officer brilliant enough to capture the killer.

The commissioner talks the detective into returning, but only on the condition that he be able to cook dinner the next night for the commissioner's wife, the old flame, who is the detective's ex-girlfriend.
After a press conference announcing the detective's reinstatement, the old flame and the detective have dinner.
Old wounds are opened, including mention of a canceled check which indicated that the commissioner was involved in the scandal that got the detective fired.
After reporting for work, the detective takes a different office than the one he was assigned because the light was not to the liking of his friend the artist, a painter.
After getting the captain to add the artist to the payroll as his assistant, the detective begins work on the case.
His first lead is to speak to the mayor's daughter, the young woman, who was a friend of the wealthy woman.
After the detective and the young woman visit the wealthy woman's apartment, he decides to let her stay at his apartment because she is too frightened to return to her own.
The detective realizes that the previous murders occurred on dates that are prime numbers, all of which are among the twelve prime numbers possible up to the number 31.
Because 5 is the only one of the prime numbers that has not been used, the detective deduces that the next murder will take place the following night, on the fifth of the month.
However, the detective is seemingly proven wrong when a woman is strangled one day ahead of the detective's prediction, after which the killer leaps out the window to his death.
The detective believes that this is a copycat killing, especially when he learns that the man broke a window, as opposed to picking a lock to gain entrance as in the other murders.
The commissioner and the mayor consider the case closed and are content to be done with the detective.
The detective and the artist discover the position of the victims' buildings, when seen on a map of the borough, forms the constellation the zodiac sign.

They also realize that all the rooms in which the murders took place have windows on the front of the building, and that when the exterior positions of the windows are lined up together according to which floor they are on, they correlate to eleven notes in the chorus of the song "the old hit".
This enables them to identify where the killer will next strike.
The detective sets a trap with the young woman as bait, outfitting her with a neck guard to prevent the killer from strangling her.
The trio stakes out the room in a supply closet and witness the killer picking the lock to get into the apartment.
They intercept the apartment's resident and send the young woman in, where she is attacked.
The detective breaks in and, after a prolonged struggle with the killer, subdues him.
He then wraps up the suspect in a carpet and delivers him to the police.
The old flame arrives and tells the detective she's broken up with the commissioner and hopes to reconcile.
He rejects her in favor of a relationship with the young woman.
A group of ten disparate people, strangers to each other, have all been summoned by a mysterious host named the unknown man to travel to the continent and join him on a safari he is hosting.
The adventurer guides the entourage with the aid of local natives through the jungle.
Things turn ominous: First their native guides abandon them, then cut the bridge line (their only way in and out of camp).
As a result, the eight guests, plus a married couple, the servants, find themselves isolated in their hunting camp.
In addition, their host, the unknown man, is absent.
Following their dinner, by means of a gramophone recording, an inhuman voice accuses each person of a murder that they had caused, for which they had escaped justice.
The young guest dies first, choking to death after drinking a poisoned martini.
His death mimics the first verse of the English nursery rhyme 'the counting rhyme'.
One of the ten Indian dolls that adorn the dining table is found with its head snapped off.
In the morning, the manservant's wife the maid is found dead in her bed (possibly from an overdose), fulfilling the second line of the rhyme.
Suspicion arises that they are being picked off by a dangerous lunatic.
As four of the men set off with rifles to hunt down the unknown man, the general is pushed off a cliff and dies.
The guests realize that "the unknown man" may be one of them.
It is discovered the radio has been sabotaged and all the ammunition are blanks.
The manservant dies next with an axe buried in his head.
The actress dies with a hypodermic syringe filled with poison.
This puts suspicion on the doctor.
The adventurer manages to repair the radio and makes contact with the outside; a spotter plane will be sent the next morning.
At night, the terrified remaining guests admit to their guilt.
A storm arrives and the judge dies, shot in the head.
The doctor dies with his throat slit.
The detective barricades himself in his tent, only to be found dead the morning after, stabbed in the chest.
By now, only the adventurer and the young woman are left, and the young woman turns on the adventurer with his gun.
He lunges at her and she shoots him.
She returns to the common tent where the judge, alive, is waiting, wearing his judicial robes and wig, with a noose prepared for her to fulfil the last verse of the rhyme.
He forces the young woman at gunpoint into the noose and explains how the doctor helped him fake his own death so he would be free to spy on the rest of the party: the "red herring" from the rhyme.
He then killed the doctor.
The judge explains that after being diagnosed with a terminal illness, he planned the safari – his own 'private, big game hunt'.
He wanted to commit murder on a grand scale and execute justice to those 'who had escaped their hangman'.
He pulls the chair out from under the young woman and watches her struggle in glee as he drinks poisoned wine to kill himself as well.
He dies and the adventurer re-appears, alive, only grazed by the bullet the young woman shot, and rescues her.
They leave together as the rescue plane arrives.
Ex-boxer the fighter is a drifter and an escapee from a mental hospital.

In a desert town near the resort city he meets widow the woman who convinces him to help fix up the neglected estate her husband left and lets him sleep in a trailer out back, near her dying date palms.
The fighter stays on the woman’s neglected property, fixing what he can and sleeping among the fading trees.
He drifts between moments of calm and flashes of memory from his boxing days and his time in the mental hospital, where overcrowding and neglect made it easy for him to escape.
The woman drinks heavily, swings between warmth and cruelty, and seems to need the fighter as much as she resents him.
Her acquaintance the con man, who claims to be an ex-cop, slowly draws the fighter into a kidnapping plan involving the boy, the sickly son of a wealthy family.
The fighter hesitates and even tries to leave, but his need to be useful and wanted keeps pulling him back.
The fighter meets the doctor, a physician who quickly recognizes the fighter’s fragile mental state and urges him to return to institutional care.
The doctor offers protection and stability, but his interest in the fighter feels controlling and intrusive, and it threatens the fighter’s bond with the woman.
Caught between the doctor’s paternal concern and the con man’s promises of money and purpose, the fighter agrees to help with the kidnapping.
The plan is carefully rehearsed, but from the start it goes wrong.
The fighter deliberately takes the wrong child first, then finally abducts the boy, who is diabetic and becomes dangerously ill without insulin.
The fighter insists the boy must be kept alive, while the con man begins to see the boy as a problem rather than a human being.
As pressure mounts, the con man reveals himself as manipulative and ruthless, willing to sacrifice the fighter to protect himself and collect reward money by playing the hero.
He also seems to owe money to a shady bartender named the barman, who may know about the kidnapping plot.
The woman goes back and forth between guilt, fear, and self-interest, at times seeming to side with the con man.
The fighter, increasingly isolated and aware that he is being used, takes control of the situation.
He steals insulin to save the boy, confronts the con man, and stops him from killing either the boy or himself.
When the doctor finds out about the kidnapping plot, the fighter accidentally kills him with a punch to the chest, which gives him a fatal heart attack.
Hiding the boy in the back of their car, the fighter and the woman follow the con man to the airport for the ransom money drop-off, but the police are lying in wait.
The con man is ambushed and killed by the barman as the police swarm in.
In the aftermath, their car is waved through the police dragnet by an unsuspecting cop who recognizes the fighter from his boxing days.
The fighter hears on the car radio that he is being sought for the murder of the doctor and for the kidnappings of both the boy and the woman.
By now, he understands that every path forward will end badly for him.
In the final moments, the fighter drives toward the inevitable, pursued by police and cut off from any future with the woman.
His last actions are deliberate and calm.
To exonerate the woman, and put all the blame on himself, he goads her into shooting him by threatening to kill the boy.
He accepts his end as the only way to give meaning to his life, by saving both the woman and the child, even if the woman never fully understands what he did for her.
When the widow's husband the businessman dies in a plane crash in the port city, the southern country, she finds that his air cargo business is deeply in the red.
When she visits the airline's terminal in the port city, she finds a packet of baseball cards that have been marked up by the businessman.
Recognizing his system for marking betting slips at race tracks, she decodes the cards and realizes that they indicate a bank account.
When she tries to withdraw money from the account, she is denied.
She realizes that the account is in the name of the player on the card, the first ballplayer.
Back home, the widow uses an International bank directory at the local library to decode the second ballplayer's baseball team's card to find another bank account in the tropical country.
She obtains durable power of attorney and begins a whirlwind trek to recover her husband's money.
After the tropical country, she visits the island nation and the island territory, recovering tens of thousands of dollars from each account.
In the European country, she closes the third ballplayer's account from the bank, but the cashier hands her only 750 DM.
He explains that 74,000DM worth of cashier's checks have been paid out to a company called the chemical firm in the former eastern city.
At the chemical firm, a manager informs the widow that they make ink for ball point pens.
The widow leaves the office confused as to why the businessman would be buying so much ink.
The manager waits for her to leave and then ushers in some men who have been following the widow on her journey.
Her next stop is the southern capital, where she finds out that the businessman's account has already been closed.
The teller takes the widow to a safe deposit box which only contains a fourth ballplayer card.
The widow's growing suspicion that the businessman is alive is confirmed by the sight of the card.
When the teller sees how distraught the widow is, she confides in her that a local shipping company cashed out some of the businessman's money and that the rest was wired to the desert capital.
She visits the shipping company and finds that one of their boats is headed to the desert capital with grain for a food aid effort.
She rides with the cargo to the desert country, and notices that one of the dock workers is being stained green by a bag of grain.
She sneaks onto the truck where he loaded the bag, opens it, and finds, hidden beneath the grain, containers of thionyl chloride manufactured by the chemical firm.
The widow soon befriends the coordinator of the relief effort, the aid worker.
She explains what she found in the bag, and the aid worker confronts his Operations Manager, who reveals that he allowed the smuggling to finance the grain shipments.
The aid worker is irate because he knows that the thionyl chloride is being used to manufacture chemical weapons.
The aid worker and the widow quickly fall in love, but she continues her journey, now intent on actually finding the businessman.
A local Immigration Agent teams up with the widow and helps her find the businessman.
He admits to the widow that he had been skimming from the chemical weapons traders, which is why he had to disappear.
When the widow leaves, the businessman runs after her and tries to make her stay with him, holding her at gunpoint in a crowded square.
The men who have been following the widow throughout the film now have the businessman in sight, and they immediately kill him.
The film ends with the widow happily back at home with her family, just as the aid worker arrives to reunite with her.
Eleven-year-old aspiring spy and writer the girl.
The girl lives a privileged life in the big city with her parents, the mother and the father, and her nanny, the governess, in whom she confides.
The girl and her best friends, the boy and the friend, are enemies with a snobby classmate, editor of the sixth-grade newspaper, bully, and class president the rival.
One night, as the girl's parents are out, the governess invites her friend the gentleman to dinner, which she burns; the three go out for dinner and a movie instead.
Upon arriving back home, the girl and the governess realize that the mother and the father have returned early.
The mother is enraged at the governess for taking the girl out without her knowledge and impulsively fires her.
The governess concedes that it is time the girl was "on her own."
Before leaving, the governess encourages the girl not to give up on her love of "spying" and observing people, promising to be the first to buy a signed copy of the girl's first novel.
Depressed and withdrawn, the girl breaks into the mansion of the rich lady and is caught hiding in her dumbwaiter.
After school, the rival discovers the girl's private spy notebook.
She begins reading aloud the girl's comments about her friends and peers, such as how she suspects the friend will grow up to be "a total nutcase" and criticizing the boy's father's low earnings.
The boy and the friend shun the girl, and her classmates create a "spy-catcher" club to torment her.
When the girl begins neglecting her schoolwork, her parents confiscate her notebooks and ask her teacher, the schoolmistress, to search her for new notebooks daily.
During art class, the rival and her friends pour blue paint over the girl as revenge for writing things about them in her notebook.
The girl responds, slapping the rival in the face, and flees from the school.

She exacts revenge in several ways: by exposing that the rival's father left their family for his secretary, by cutting off a chunk of the classmate's hair, by sabotaging the friend's science experiment, and by humiliating the boy with a picture of him in a maid's outfit.
This causes her classmates to alienate her further.
The girl's parents send her for a psychological evaluation; the doctor assures them that the girl is fine.
The girl gets her notebook back, and, in a surprise visit, the governess tells her that to make things right again, she must do two things that she will not like: apologize and lie.
The girl says it is not worth it, to which the governess disagrees, saying the girl is worth it as an individual, and her individuality will make others nervous.
She adds: "Good friends are one of life's blessings.
Don't give them up without a fight."

The girl tries apologizing to the boy and the friend, who initially rejected her before accepting her apology after finally coming to their senses and consequently quitting the rival's bully group due to being mistreated by her, much to the rival's dismay.
The girl opines to the schoolmistress that the rival's appointment as editor was done unfairly, and the schoolmistress opens it up for a vote.
The girl is voted in to replace the rival as editor.
She writes an article apologizing to the class, all of whom (except the rival) accept her apology.
At the opening of the 6th-grade pageant, the friend, the boy, and the girl set off a stink bomb as all the students, teachers, and audience dance to the soul singer's "the funk song."
The detective has married the heiress, the rich daughter of local tycoon the magnate.
The heiress and the detective first met in the earlier novel and their romance is resumed at the end of the previous novel.

The detective resists financial dependence on his willing wife and, after the couple relocate to a grand mansion in the resort town (a mocking reference to the real resort city), opens a detective agency in the resort.
Tension between them rises when, as a result, the detective absents himself from the cocktail parties and other social events organised by the heiress’s set.

The detective’s first case comes when he is forced by hoodlums to visit a local criminal named the casino operator, who operates an illegal gambling house in the neighbouring city, just outside the jurisdiction of the resort town.
He has taken an IOU for $100,000 from one of his customers, a resort town photographer called the debtor.
The casino operator's boss, an unrevealed local tycoon, has found out that the sum is missing from the books and has issued a 30-day ultimatum to retrieve the money.
Asked to find the debtor, the detective accepts on condition that he does not have to shake the debtor down.
When the detective questions the debtor's wife, the society wife, a spoiled socialite and acquaintance of his own wife, she tells him that the debtor is out on a photo shoot.
Instead he eventually discovers that the debtor is an alias for a sleazy individual living in the big city with a second wife.

When the detective calls on the casino operator again, he finds him killed in his casino office and assists the debtor to escape after he is suspected, not just for this crime but for an earlier slaying in his own office.
The melodramatic pay-off exposes the corruption of the regional rich and confirms the detective in his decision to return to the big city.
His marriage is wrecked, but he and the heiress remain as lovers.
The protagonist is a young American woman living in the city who believes she is happy in a secure job and a relationship with her boyfriend.
After a chance encounter with a mysterious stranger, she seeks him out, taking a taxi with him to his house and having passionate sex.
She returns home to her boyfriend and unsuccessfully attempts to bring out the same feelings between them that she had with the strange man.

The following day she seeks the stranger out again, discovering he is the climber - a mountain climber who is considered a hero after saving six people in a tragic event that killed several others, including the woman he loved.
The protagonist leaves her boyfriend and begins a relationship with the climber, although her friend shows reservations about the protagonist being in such a sudden relationship.
When the protagonist is mugged on the street, the climber beats the thief terribly, and then asks the protagonist to marry him, a proposal she happily accepts.
For their honeymoon, he takes her to a secluded cabin.
The newlyweds settle into their new life, but the protagonist is troubled by a series of mysterious letters and phone calls, and begins to wonder about her husband's mysterious past.
A reporter who did a story on the climber sends her a copy of a letter from a woman claiming the climber raped her.
The protagonist interviews her, posing as a journalist.

Disturbed by the fact that she barely knows her new husband, she begins to go through their apartment, becoming even more alarmed when she searches a locked wardrobe and finds a box of old letters from an ex-lover, the former lover, who insists she and the climber end their affair.
The climber begins to question the protagonist more about her activities, including where she got a necklace that she received from his sister, the sister.
Soon after, the protagonist receives yet another warning.
Following the trail, she discovers that the former lover has been missing for eight months.
She also finds a picture of the former lover at the same cabin where she and the climber honeymooned.
She realizes she doesn't feel safe with him and runs to the police.
She tells her story, insisting they reopen the former lover's missing persons case, but they can't do anything without any evidence, telling her they can only keep him for a few hours.
The protagonist seeks help from the sister, telling her she believes the climber killed the former lover for leaving him and buried her at the cabin.
On the way to the cabin, the sister admits that she was the one who sent the messages to the protagonist, because she wanted to save her from the climber's violent rages.
When the climber returns home from the police station, he finds that the protagonist was there and left the two pictures, and realizes she must have gone to the cemetery.
At the cemetery, the protagonist discovers a body buried in the dirt, wearing the same necklace that the sister gave her.
The sister tells her that the former lover didn't have to die, if only she had told her she was going back to her husband.
The sister revealed that she had sex with the climber when he was 15 years old, resulting in her subsequent obsession with her own brother and need to rid his life of any other woman.
She tries to kill the protagonist, but the climber appears in time and saves her.
Furious, the sister tries to kill him but is stopped short by the protagonist, who shoots her with a flare pistol.
The climber tells the protagonist that he and his sister used to come to the cabin together, but that he thought that if the protagonist just trusted him, then everything would be alright.
The climber is led away by police that morning.
Two years later, the protagonist and the climber see one another again on either side of an escalator - she's going down and he's riding up.
They both watch each other as they pass without saying anything.
The climber stops at the top and turns to stare back at the protagonist before walking away.
The film ends with the protagonist's voiceover recalling the events in posterity and wondering what might have happened had fate not led her to the climber one morning.
She wonders if the passion between them could ever have lasted, and if a "flatlander" like her could ever have stayed at such a high altitude.
Mourning the pope's sudden death, the church prepares the papal conclave to elect his successor.
The papal aide, the Camerlengo, temporarily controls the city-state during the sede vacante.
Meanwhile, at the research laboratory, scientists.
The priest scientist and the physicist create three antimatter canisters.
Checking on them, the physicist finds the priest scientist murdered and one canister gone.
Shortly thereafter, four preferiti are kidnapped by a supposed secret society representative.
The city-state discovers one cardinal will die each hour, from 8 p.m. to midnight, when the antimatter explodes, destroying the city.
The envoy recruits American symbologist the professor to help, for his experience with the secret order in one capital and another capital.
He deduces the four murders will occur on the four altars of the "secret path", relevant to the classical elements.
The professor is granted access to the city-state's secret archive to research the altars, against the head of the papal guard the commander's wishes.
An astronomer's banned book gives clues to the first altar.
Initially believing it is the ancient temple, they realise it is the chapel.
The commander dismissively abandons them, but two city-state police officers rush them there.
Too late, the first cardinal has suffocated through a mouth full of dirt, and is branded with "Earth".
A clue at the chapel's old master statue leads the professor to the next altar, another sculpture in the main square.
Again arriving late, the second cardinal's lungs are punctured and he is branded with "Air".
A note left makes the physicist suspect the pope's "stroke" was actually a tinzaparin overdose, which they secretly confirm this inspecting his body in the necropolis.
The professor and the officers hurry to the altar of fire, the basilica.
The third cardinal has been burned to death, branded with "Fire".
The assassin then kills all but the professor before escaping.
The final altar is the plaza's fountain sculpture.
The incompetent commander demands the professor return to the city-state, but he and two policemen catch the assassin drowning the fourth cardinal, who is branded with "Water", in a fountain.
He kills the officers and escapes, but the professor and bystanders rescue the fourth cardinal.
He reveals the preferiti were held in the old fortress.
When the commander confiscates the priest scientist's journals, the physicist believes he is involved.
She and the professor storm the old fortress, the assassin's lair, find the four brands, and deduce a missing fifth one is meant for the papal aide.
The assassin confronts them, but leaves them both unharmed.
He insists clergy hired him, suggesting they "be careful".
The assassin's anonymous contact guides him to a bomb-rigged escape car.
The professor and the physicist find a secret passageway to the city-state, warning the papal guard of the papal aide's fate.
They find the commander hovering over a branded papal aide.
The papal guard shoot and kill him and alleged co-conspirator the archbishop.
The professor retrieves a key from the dying commander's hand.
The antimatter container is found in the saint's tomb, set to detonate in five minutes.
As the cold temperature has prematurely drained the battery keeping the antimatter in suspension, it will not reach midnight.
So, former helicopter pilot the papal aide flies the canister into the sky, parachuting out seconds before the antimatter detonates.
This unleashes a powerful, blinding shockwave throughout the city-state, but no one dies and the church is saved.
Hailed a hero, there are calls to elect him pope by acclamation.
The professor and the physicist discover the priest scientist's journals reference hidden security cameras monitoring the Pope for medical reasons.
With the commander's key, they find footage showing the papal aide masterminded the attacks.
